subject: snail
pitch: A garden snail on an adventure. A glossy spiral shell striped in caramel, chocolate and cream, a soft grey-green body with a pebbly texture and a slimy shine, two long eye stalks with little black eyes and two short feelers below. A tiny ladybird hitches a ride on top of the shell.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the snail's proportions, aiming for a realistic garden snail scale with a shell around 3.5cm and a body length of about 8cm, oriented facing forward along the Z-axis. Now I'm sketching out the skeleton structure to build it on.

Building the body sweep...

Still defining the body taper...

Still building the skeleton...

Adding short feelers below the eye stalks with base-mid-tip points angled forward-outward, tapering radius. For the shell, I'm planning a logarithmic spiral coil with growing tube radius to mimic a snail shell shape.

I need the shell's coil axis tilted sideways with the spiral starting at the outer opening and shrinking inward, scaling tube radius down to keep the shell proportional to the body size (~3-4cm shell vs 6-8cm body).

Working out the whorl geometry so each loop sits tightly against the next, cone-like, with the tube radius scaling proportionally to the coil radius at each turn so the whorls appear to touch realistically from the side.

Checking the geometry with tube radius around 0.52r, I verify adjacent whorls stay close enough to overlap and form a solid shell while spiraling inward and advancing along the axis toward the apex.

Now I'm thinking about shell orientation — the big opening whorl sits near the body with the apex pointing outward along the axis. For a dextral garden snail, I want the axis tilted so the spiral reads correctly from the side, with the apex bulging toward one side of the view.

I'm placing the outer whorl where it meets the body's back, then working out the coil geometry: the spiral plane runs mostly through y and z, with the tube radius and whorl radius determining how tall the shell stands above the body and how far it dips in. I'm nudging the center height so the shell top clears the body while the bottom tucks slightly in, and shifting the spiral start along x so the apex extends outward properly.

I'm now computing the perpendicular direction to the coil axis so the starting point of the spiral sits correctly in the right plane, using a cross product against a basis vector to derive that offset.

The tube's start point stays mostly hidden inside the body, which works fine. For stripes, I want them to run along the spiral direction rather than across it, so I'll paint color bands based on the clock angle around the tube's cross-section instead of the position along it—giving caramel, chocolate, and cream bands that follow the whorls naturally.

Defining the stripe bands...

I also want to add fine growth lines modulated along the body axis, darkening periodically for texture. Since the paint material's roughness and shininess are shared across body and shell meshes, I'll need to figure out whether I can adjust glossiness per-mesh or if I have to work within the shared material constraints.

Since the log spiral's arc length is roughly proportional to radius, I can approximate the radius as linear in arc fraction, giving a simple interpolation from r0 to r1. I'm parenting the shell joint to the mid-spine bone and will need a surface point at the shell's top for placing the ladybird on it.

I'm firing a downward ray from above the shell to find a surface point for the ladybird's position and orientation, then building its hemisphere body (a scaled, partial sphere geometry) along with head, spots, and tiny legs, parented to the shell joint and sunk slightly into the surface for a natural resting look.

Now I'm adding details: a thin black box for the elytra split line along the dome's top, and placing small flattened black spheres as spots using the dome's curvature formula to compute their height at chosen x,z offsets.

For the head, a small black sphere with tiny white eye dots sits at the front, and I'm considering skipping legs and pronotum patches to keep things modest, maybe adding thin antenna boxes instead. Since the real ladybird is only 7mm against an 8cm model, I'll scale it up by about 1.4x for visibility, and orient it facing forward along +z to match the shell's direction.

Now I'm working out the shell's spiral placement — setting the center point, calculating the apex position from the pitch and turn count along a normalized axis, and checking the resulting x-span. This reveals the shell ends up offset to the left relative to the body's half-width, which I need to account for so it doesn't overhang awkwardly.

Checking the whorl tube dimensions against the start position, making sure the bottom of the first whorl stays consistent with the body's shape near the apex transition.

Verifying the spiral doesn't overlap the body oddly, and sanity-checking the ladybird ray sampling against the surface mesh world matrices. I'm considering whether to add a subtle slime trail beneath the foot, maybe a thin pale translucent strip, but it might be unnecessary polish I can skip.

Adding slime trail sweep...

Now I'm layering countershading between the darker back and lighter belly, deciding to skip a separate dorsal stripe for simplicity. I'm working out the eyestalk geometry—base, midpoint, and tip positions for each stalk coming off the head, with small eyeball spheres placed at the tips.

I'm setting up the spine as a catmull-smoothed chain of six points for five body spans, then sweeping it with a tapered radius to build the body shape. Next I'm adding a jaw joint parented to the head tip to prepare for mouth articulation.

Now I'm computing where the mouth should sit on the tapered head cone, using the surface ellipse equation to figure out the right z-depth at that height, then placing upper and lower lip boxes slightly protruding at that spot, one anchored to the head and one to the jaw bone.

I'm also planning a small dark mouth pit box for depth, naming joint chains with left/right mirroring using a sign multiplier, tagging feeler bones with a "tentacle" role, and bumping the shell sweep sides up to 10 for smoother curves before writing the actual code.

Now I'm working out the shell's spiral geometry: computing a flattened "down" direction orthogonal to the shell axis, deriving the starting point, and generating a spiral sweep with set turns, radius, and pitch, attaching it as a joint parented to the spine. I'm also figuring out the shell coloring logic so that caramel stripes wrap continuously around the whorls based on angle and position along the spiral.

Writing shell paint colors...

Now I'm setting up the ladybird positioning by casting a ray downward to find where it lands on the surface, with a fallback position if the ray misses.

Building the ladybird's body geometry: a scaled dome for the shell, plus a flattened black sphere underneath for the belly, all positioned relative to the landing point.

I'm placing dark spots along the dome's curved surface using a formula derived from the sphere's radius, then adding a seam made of small boxes stepping along the shell's curve to mimic the central ladybird line. For the head, I'm adding a small flattened black sphere with white eye dots.

Now I'm positioning thin leg boxes angled downward in pairs along the body, then checking overall bounds so the sole and slime trail sit flush with the ground. I'm defining the sole's sweep path with tapering radii so it narrows toward the tail.

Still writing sweep function...

The bottom taper is fine since it's covered by the sole, and the head doesn't need a separate sphere, just a rounded end cap with a small snout bump. At the end I'll traverse the root mesh to bump up roughness on any paint material, then return the root before writing out the final code.
